title: Is it realistic to expect an open-source GitHub for an AI-extracted RTS pathfinding engine soon?
author: Aeduh
selftext:
With the recent boom in AI-driven binary deconstruction pipelines (connecting agents via MCP to tools like Ghidra and LLMs for exact code-matching reverse engineering), I’ve been thinking about its application to RTS navigation.

Right now, the holy grail of RTS development is pathfinding that can handle thousands of dynamic units with zero-allocation CPU footprints, proper dynamic bumping, and fluid crowd movement. Historically, indie devs have to build this from scratch or rely on academic implementations of A* or JPS+ that don’t quite capture the "secret sauce" of triple-A engines.

We know the industry giants already solved this decades ago, for example:

 - StarCraft II mastered pixel-perfect, hyper-reactive local avoidance and dynamic bumping on complex NavMeshes.

 - Supreme Commander 2 popularized commercial Flow Fields (Continuum Crowds) to move massive armies with flat CPU costs.

 - Total War perfected hierarchical systems (HPA*) for maintaining rigid yet organic military formations.

Given that AI agents are becoming incredibly good at isolating assembly routines, abstracting the core mathematical logic from compiled executables, and rewriting them into modern high-performance code (like Rust or Data-Oriented C++):

Do you think it's realistic to expect a community-driven, open-source "Frankenstein" pathfinding library soon?

I’m talking about an engine agnostic library born from AI reverse-engineering diverse legacy binaries, using a Clean Room design approach to strip away proprietary code and metadata while preserving the core micro-optimizations that made those classic games run beautifully.

Are there any active public pipelines or repos exploring this specific use case right now, or are legal guardrails and DMCA fears going to keep this tech locked away in modding Discords? Would love to hear your thoughts on the technical feasibility and timeline.

replies.author: DeProgrammer99
replies.body:
This is true. The complexity and probably the main reason there's no general solution is that every game takes a different set of attributes into account:

Unit size

Turn radius, which could also depend on speed, which then means acceleration/deceleration may need taken into account

Fog of war or line of sight

Height, swamps, known enemy territory, and other terrain with different costs

Allowed trajectories (like SC1 was 8-directional)

The approach to the map in the first place could be square tiles, diamonds, just arbitrarily located nodes, a large number of sparsely connected nodes or islands, etc.)

Also its memory structure

Behavior for known immobile units that are in the way, in contrast to mobile ones, possibly different for foes, possibly also different for allies or neutral units

Changes over time, such as closing off or newly opening paths, units dying, aircraft taking off

How perfect you want the unit's intelligence to appear--does it beeline straight to the correct path or need to adjust a few times as it gets closer?

And I'm sure there are plenty of others I didn't think of off the top of my head just now.

comments.author: Pannoniae

youre coping, games usually have solutions customised for either own needs. sc2 works with their units' turning speed, AI and unit count, supreme commander / other TA-likes have different needs, total war is big on units which consist of individual soldiers, etc.

unless you want to make exactly the same game, they wont help you. the legal stuff is fairly irrelevant compared to the practical barriers. if it was a significant factor then there would be much more focus on IP protection and proactively eliminating competition.

also, general-purpose open source libraries will always suck compared to a specialised solution. the core tech is well-known, implement it then specialise it according to your needs ;)
